newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-China the wild card in turbulent world zinc.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-China the wild card in turbulent world zinc.

text.p: The price of zinc is making wild gyrations in the latest turmoil to hit a world market perplexed by the enigmatic China Factor.
Speculators in the West find that it just isn't easy to read China's hand as the Chinese emerge among decisive players in the international commodity markets.
Last year China suddenly turned around sagging freight rates when it unexpectedly began to import big volumes of fertiliser.

China also became a force in copper in recent years, taking huge positions but losing, traders said, when the market collapsed with news of $2.6 billion unauthorised trading losses by Japan's Sumitomo Corp in June 1996.
The focus in zinc has been a view that Chinese smelters were short of metal to deliver, so that prices on the London Metal Exchange rallied to hit a seven-year high at $1,675 per tonne on Monday.
A sell-off led by speculative funds has now taken the price down towards $1,450, fuelled by a suspicion, which several analysts think is correct, that the Chinese position has eased.
"The Chinese have tried to spread the risk by exchanging 3-months zinc commitments for contracts based on the annual average for 1998," one analyst said.

A residual short position still exists, and this may account for a firm premium of cash over three-months delivery, but most of 250,000 tonnes that the Chinese were due to deliver in September has been covered or rolled forward, according to these analysts and LME traders.
They added, however, that by using futures and options to delay squaring up their positions, Chinese smelters were setting themselves up for future squeezes and further losses.
The strategy of buying call options with a strike price of $1,450-$1,650 to lock in losses had also failed to extricate the Chinese from their predicament, the analysts said.

Comments by the Chinese zinc industry during the recent turmoil in zinc have been seen as contradictory. But the analysts saw this as the result of ill-conceived trading strategies rather than an attempt to manipulate price levels, although increased prices have brought higher revenues in Chinese physical trade.
"It did not make sense for a net exporter to talk down the market by announcing increases in production unless they had over committed themselves," an analyst said.
Traders said they were mystified. "It is very difficult to know what to believe in terms of what comes out of China," one said.
"The zinc market has been a wild old beast. These moves have done a lot of damage to the market," said another.
Zinc traded to a low of $1,410 early on Thursday before bouncing back to over $1,450 and the market is expected to continue volatile.
Alan Williamson of Bain and Co said zinc was likely to find a range of $1,350-$1,400. "Anything above $1,400 during the summer slowdown is just a bit of a bubble," he added.
"In the short term zinc is likely to remain volatile with a bias for the upside," said Martin Squires of Rudolf Wolff.
Asian traders and Chinese industry sources said on Thursday they expected prices to stabilise around $1,400 to $1,450 a tonne, or even drop lower in the immediate term.
"It should drop from here, I think $1,400 or below would be more reasonable," a Chinese metals industry executive said.

"I don't think it will go ballistic again; it is happy around here between $1,400-1,450," the Singapore trader said, though he added: "It all depends on the funds, it could be at $2,000 by the end of the year."

Fundamentals, including falling world stocks, rising demand on good worldwide economic growth, and increasing production of galvanized steel, had long pointed to rises in the zinc price to about $1,450 a tonne, analysts have said.
But the signals were either missed or misinterpreted by Chinese metals industry leaders, who in late 1996 directed smelters to sell forward once the price reached levels around $1,100.
And sell forward they did, to the tune of about 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes, according to sources in Beijing's metals production arm China National Nonferrous Metals Corp (CNNC).
Some Chinese forward selling had been done at $1,280 and $1,350, one source said.
The turbulence in zinc has also impacted on the other base metals, in particular copper and aluminium.

Traders said that copper was "ominously quiet" early on Thursday, and with a contraction in the backwardation to around $30, traders said they expected a price slide to $2,200, from $2,300 on Thursday. -- London Newsroom + 44 171 542 8071
